title: Did the brains get better? Round 3's eras, with more coins

thesis.claim: Round 3's brains got better early and had stopped getting better by the middle of their runs; and how much a world's brains got better follows its place in the evolution rank, not its health. In most of the worlds the brains of every later era beat those of iteration 250 beyond a contest's own noise; against the brains of iteration 1,500, the eras after it do no better than that noise; and the worlds the rank puts first gained the most.
thesis.why: On the brain-copy tree, where conquests make 58% of the copies in the median world, round 3's worlds live through about 2,700 generations in 3,000 iterations, and their ancestry narrows far faster than chance allows: in 69 of the 82 worlds that lived, the living meet one ancestor sooner than in any of 100 shadow worlds of random parents (Candidates for open-ended evolution). Selection on what the brains do is beyond chance almost everywhere, yet the line of descent moves less than mutation alone would move it in 79 of the 82 worlds (Did evolution happen? Fourteen ways to find out): the brains are held in place, as they are once selection has found what it can. The notebook's two longest worlds, of B2 with brains mixed at birth, climbed for 20,000 to 25,000 iterations and then only wandered (Every era against three, Experiment 28); round 3's worlds copy brains several times as often, so they should reach their plateau within their 3,000 iterations. The evolution rank reads what an improvement needs: lines that spread beyond what luck spreads, behaviour new beyond what mutation alone makes, brains copied in proportion to what they do, and children that play like their parents. Health reads the shape of a world, and is unrelated to the rank (rank correlation -0.01). Against this: some lines never return to behaviour they had shown, so some worlds may still climb at the end; and eight of the rank's first ten stake a token at a time, for which two of its four readings are only approximations.
thesis.confirm: All three. (1) In at least two thirds of the worlds, the median score of the eras 500 to 3,000 against 250 lies above the world's noise band: above 0.5 plus twice the standard deviation of its twelve contests of an era against itself (250, 1,500 and 3,000, four coins each). An era's score is the share of the agents that hold the later era's brains at the end, the mean of its six contests, three coins on each era's world. (2) In at least two thirds of the worlds, the median score of the eras 2,000 to 3,000 against 1,500 lies within the band, between 0.5 minus and 0.5 plus twice that deviation. (3) A world's gain is the median score of its eras 500 to 3,000 against 250. Across the worlds, the gain rises with the evolution rank's score (research/screen/evolution.json of 12 November 2026): Spearman's rho above 0, with a one-sided permutation p below 0.05 (10,000 permutations); and the gain's rho with health's product is smaller than its rho with the evolution score.
thesis.refute: Any of: (1) in fewer than half of the worlds do the eras 500 to 3,000 score above the band against 250, so most worlds did not get better at all; (2) in half of the worlds or more, the eras 2,000 to 3,000 score above the band against 1,500, so most were still getting better in the middle of their runs; (3) the gain does not rise with the evolution score (rho at 0 or below), or its rho with health's product is larger. Between these, the thesis is undecided. A world whose contests cannot be played decides nothing and is left out of every count.
